headline: Iradiya adds one E190 as cover for two rotations; winter timetable unchanged
dek: The new jet has lie-flat business seats, but any second weekly flight to Dubai or Istanbul would need fresh permits, and none is applied for before summer 2027.
paragraphs: Iradiya (Irad Air Services) took delivery on Sunday 22 November of one additional Embraer E190, which will back up its Monday Dubai and Friday Istanbul charter rotations. Both have so far been flown with a single jet each. The winter 2026/27 timetable, in force from 25 October to 27 March, does not change.

The aircraft reached the Talas Civil Air Terminal on a delivery flight. Like every Iradiya flight, it needed landing and overflight permits from the neighbours, none of which recognises the Irad Special Economic Zone. Kamila Rakhmatova, duty manager of the terminal, confirmed the arrival and said the airline's published schedule stands. "The aircraft came in on Sunday and the winter timetable is as published," she said. "Passengers will see no change on the board."

The jet has a refitted black-and-burgundy cabin with lie-flat seats in business class. It is the first aircraft in the Iradiya fleet with them, according to the airline. It goes into service as cover for IRD 721/722 to Dubai and IRD 711/712 to Istanbul, the latter with its technical stop at Baku. If the jet that normally flies one of those rotations is out of service, the spare can take its place without a cancellation.

Cover is not capacity. The international flights from Talas are charters, flown as weekly series, and each series is authorised separately. A second weekly frequency to either city would be a new series needing new permits. Transport Minister Oleg Rudenko said no such application has been made. "Each series stands on its own landing and overflight permits," he said. "We have applied for nothing beyond the published timetable before summer 2027."

IradOne reported on Thursday that the terminal has room to grow and that summer 2027 routes hinge on permits. The government said in a statement the same day that the terminal has space for planning ahead. Neither said which neighbour would have to agree to what, and the permits are not published.

Prof. Raisa Akmatova, an economist at Talas State University, said a spare aircraft saves the airline more than it earns. "A cancelled charter means stranded passengers and a new permit request for the replacement date," she said. "One more jet makes the present schedule more reliable. It is not a new market." She added that the lease terms, the aircraft's registry and the price paid have not been made public, so the cost of the cover cannot be judged.

Passengers had their own views. Rustam Aliev, 25, who repairs phones at a counter in Talas and moved from Nurzhan in October, said a cousin buys parts in Dubai and has twice had to rebook when the Monday flight changed aircraft. "For me the seats do not matter," he said. "I only want the flight to go on Monday." He added that his Iradi is chala and that he reads the departures board in English.

Iradiya and the Ministry of Transport had not answered questions on the lease, the registry or the cost of the refit by the time this edition went to press. The domestic Talas–Tash-Kömür flight, IRD 301/302, continues to be flown by an ATR 72. The ministry and the terminal say the next point for new frequencies is the summer 2027 planning round.
